name: Rosa Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I pack orders at a medicines wholesaler on the industrial estate behind the hospital, eight till half four. Chemists order paracetamol, plasters, baby formula, and I pick them off the shelves into blue tote boxes. Every box has a batch number, and the scanner beeps at you if you grab the wrong strength. The vans go out twice a day, so the morning is a rush and the afternoon is calmer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the routine. Same people, same aisles, same tea break at ten, and I know where everything is. What wears me out is the look-alike boxes, two strengths of the same tablet in nearly the same packet, and I still get those wrong after three years. My supervisor, Glenda, has had words with me about it twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never believed it anyway. I'd probably say it to Diego, my boyfriend, over dinner, and to the girls at tea break. I don't go online about things like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's nothing much. Medicines don't stop. People get headaches whether AI works or not, and somebody has to put the paracetamol in the box. I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep going in, keep putting a bit aside each month, maybe a hundred and fifty, and we've got about three months saved. I might finally try harder on the look-alike boxes so Glenda stops checking my totes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable. That's how I like things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life that worries you, even in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, a bit, it went up again in the summer. But Diego drives buses and we both have steady hours, so we're all right. My mum lives ten minutes away, so if something happened we'd have somewhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever look for a better-paid job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I've moved jobs before and the first months are horrible, you don't know anyone and you're always wrong. Here I know where the plasters are with my eyes closed.

say: I'd say I **never believed** the AI talk anyway.
I'd say it to Diego and the **tea break** group, not online.
think: **Medicines** are always needed, so my packing job stays.
I'd be **fine** if things carried on as they are.
do: Keep going in and save about **a hundred and fifty** a month.
Try harder on the **look-alike boxes** so my supervisor stops checking my totes.
feel: **Comfortable**, which is exactly how she likes things.
S0.quote: Medicines don't stop. People get headaches whether AI works or not, and somebody has to put the paracetamol in the box.
fieldNote: She values **routine** above pay and dreads starting somewhere new.
Her household has two **steady wages** and a mother nearby as backup.
Her one work worry is **picking errors** on similar packets.

steps.text: Keep packing chemist orders on the day shift
Save about a hundred and fifty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office lot who need to worry, not us on the floor. Somebody still has to lift the boxes. I'd say that at tea break and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ordering and the invoices would go to the computer, so the girls in the office might lose hours. The robots would come for us slower, maybe a machine that picks the tablets. I'm not the kind to run at the first rumour. I'll learn the new thing when I'm told to, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and keep my head down. I'd save a bit more, maybe two hundred a month instead of one fifty. If they brought in new scanners or screens I'd do the training they give us, but I wouldn't go looking for courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not scared, but I'd notice the empty desks in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pam in the office, she does the chemist orders over the phone. If the computer takes the orders, I don't know what she'd do, she's been there twenty years. She's the one who brings cake on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Diego?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buses that drive themselves, I've heard about that. Diego says it'll never happen on our roads with the parked cars and the school run. I hope he's right.

say: I'd say the **office staff** need to worry, not the people lifting boxes.
I'd keep it to **tea break** chat and leave it there.
think: Ordering and invoices go to **software** first, so office hours shrink.
I won't **run at rumours**; I'll learn new things only when told to.
do: Raise savings from one fifty to **two hundred** a month.
Do any **training** the company provides, but not look for courses myself.
feel: **Uneasy**, noticing empty desks in the office.
S1.quote: I'm not the kind to run at the first rumour. I'll learn the new thing when I'm told to, not before.
fieldNote: She correctly sees **office work** going first and her packing later.
She worries for her colleague Pam, who takes **phone orders**.
Her boyfriend Diego's **bus job** is a quiet second worry she half-dismisses.

steps.text: Raise monthly savings to two hundred
Do only the scanner training the company gives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness to let it happen that fast. Somebody in government should slow it down. I'd say it to my mum and to anyone at work who'd listen, but I wouldn't march or anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and the office is gone, then by 2031 there's a machine that can pick tablets as well as me. And Diego's buses would be driving themselves by then too. If robots take my packing job and the buses drive themselves, my boyfriend Diego and I are both out in the same year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all extras straight away, no holiday, no new phone, and try to get to six months saved. I'd talk to my mum about moving back in with her for a while if we had to. I'd keep going to work every day until they told me not to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at retraining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd even train for. I left school before my exams. If someone told me exactly what course and it was close to home, maybe, but I wouldn't know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving back with your mum be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small. She's got a two-bedroom flat and my little brother's still in the second room. Diego would hate it, but it's better than a bill we can't pay.

say: I'd say it's **madness** to let AI arrive that fast.
I'd tell my mum and colleagues the government should **slow it down**, but not march.
think: By 2031 a machine **picks tablets** as well as me.
Diego's **bus job** could go the same year, leaving both of us out.
do: Cut **holidays and phones** and aim for six months saved.
Talk to my mum about **moving in** with her if needed.
S2.quote: If robots take my packing job and the buses drive themselves, my boyfriend Diego and I are both out in the same year.
fieldNote: The **double hit** to both household earners is what alarms her.
She has **no retraining idea** and would need someone to point the way.
Her fallback is **family**: her mother's small flat.

steps.text: Cancel the summer holiday and the new phone
Build savings up to six months of bills
Ask her mum about moving into the spare room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for the companies to sort out something for their workers. I'd expect the government to make them. I'd say that at work, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office goes by 2031 and the floor by about 2034. That's long enough that I'd get used to the idea, but I still wouldn't know what I'd do after. I'd keep packing until the day they wheel the robot in, and I'd have the savings ready for that day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save, mainly, and keep my record clean at work so I'm not first out. I'd ask Glenda what the company plans for us, once. If they offered a course on running the machines I'd take it, as long as it was in work hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried in the background. Like a dentist appointment months away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait until they wheel the robot in. Is that a choice or a habit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both, I suppose. Every time I've changed something, it's gone worse for a while. So I wait, and sometimes waiting has worked out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Diego think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says five years is ages and I worry too much. But he's also asked his depot about training on the electric buses, so he's not that relaxed.

say: I'd say five years is enough for **companies** to look after their workers.
I'd expect the **government** to make them do it.
think: The office goes by **2031** and the floor by about **2034**.
I'd keep packing until the **robot arrives**, with savings ready for that day.
do: Keep my **work record clean** so I'm not first out.
Ask Glenda **once** about the company's plans and take a course only in work hours.
feel: **Worried** in the background, like a dentist appointment months away.
S3.quote: I'd keep packing until the day they wheel the robot in, and I'd have the savings ready for that day.
fieldNote: Her **waiting** is part habit, part lesson from past changes going badly.
Five years gives her time to **save**, not to change course.
Diego is quietly **preparing** more than he admits.

steps.text: Keep the tote error rate down to avoid being first out
Ask Glenda what the company plans for packers
Keep saving two hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a long way off and there's no point panicking. I'd say it at tea break if it came up. Mostly I wouldn't bring it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is longer than I've had any job, so I can't get worked up about 2039. I'd be forty. Maybe by then Diego and I have a bit more saved and it's less scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing in the first year, honestly. Keep working, keep saving. If the people around me started retraining, I might follow them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little itch at the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind and act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Glenda or the manager said something official. Rumours I ignore, but a letter I'd read. Or if my mum started worrying, she worries for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd plan differently with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd stay in the flat instead of moving to a bigger one. A bigger rent with all this coming feels silly. That's about it.

say: I'd say it's **a long way off** and there's no point panicking.
I'd mention it at **tea break** only if someone else did.
think: Ten years is **longer than any job** I've had, so 2039 feels distant.
By forty we might have **more saved**, making it less scary.
do: Keep **working and saving** with nothing new in the first year.
**Follow colleagues** into retraining if they start first.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a small **itch** at the back of her mind.
S4.quote: Ten years is longer than I've had any job, so I can't get worked up about 2039.
fieldNote: Distance makes her **dismiss** the threat, consistent with her resistant style.
She'd act only on an **official letter**, not rumours.
She'd **stay put** in the current flat rather than take on more rent.

steps.text: Wait for an official word from the company before acting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Diego and I would both be out at once with no time to think. What would help is someone telling us exactly what to train for, close to home, and money to live on while we do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who don't like change. Everyone talks about the clever ones who'll be fine. I don't need to love the new world. I just need a place in it where I can still pay the rent.

headlineQuote: I don't need to love the new world. I just need a place in it where I can still pay the rent.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old packer** at a medicines wholesaler who loves routine and still mixes up look-alike boxes.
She is **pragmatic** and slow to change, and waits for official word before acting.
She lives with her boyfriend Diego, a **bus driver**, and her mother nearby is her fallback.
She is **calm** in a plateau but **alarmed** by fast AGI, when both household jobs could go.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when she and Diego could both lose work in the same year.
whatWouldHelp: Clear advice on **what to train for**, close to home, with money to live on meanwhile.
